stemMd: According to the passage, the expectation account of promising explains **too much** because
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: only the promisee, and not a third party, may release the promisor.

options.label: B
options.textMd: a confident prediction can create reliance without binding the person who makes it.

options.label: C
options.textMd: a promise that nobody heard seems to bind less firmly than one that was heard.

options.label: D
options.textMd: a promise binds even a promisee who has not relied on it at all.

explanationMd:
The second paragraph makes a two-part criticism and labels each half. Locate the label first, then read only the clause attached to it.

"Too much" is glossed immediately: *because a confident prediction — "the ferry will run tomorrow" — can create reliance just as effectively without binding the person who makes it to anything at all.* The complaint is that reliance is present in a case where obligation is absent, so reliance cannot be what generates obligation. Option B restates this.

**How to check.** The paragraph is deliberately symmetrical: "too much" is followed by one clause and "too little" by another. Cover the option list and finish the sentence "too much, because…" from the passage in your own words; then find the option that matches. If your sentence mentions a promisee who has *not* relied, you have finished the other half of the criticism, which the passage attaches to "too little".

distractorRationale.d: This is the passage's 'too little' complaint, not its 'too much' complaint. It describes a case where obligation is present but reliance is absent, which is the mirror image of what the question asks about. The option is right about the passage and wrong about which half of the criticism it belongs to.
distractorRationale.c: The passage offers this as a point in the expectation account's *favour* — the reason the account is 'attractive' — not as a defect. This option takes the merit stated at the start of the paragraph and presents it as the objection stated later in it.
distractorRationale.a: Release by the promisee belongs to the third paragraph, where it is the feature the *second* account explains and the expectation theory struggles with. It is not part of the 'too much' objection at all.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying philosophy passage on promising, asking why the passage says the expectation account of promising explains too much.

provenance.notes: Original item written against an original passage.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The passage says 'Too much, because a confident prediction ... can create reliance ... without binding', which is (b). (d) is the passage's 'too little' point (the wealthy promisee who did not rely). (c) is why the account is attractive. (a) is the feature the second account explains.

Option A is the paired 'too little' clause, B is the merit conceded earlier in the same paragraph, and C belongs to paragraph 3. Awaiting a blind independent solve before publication.
